body.en:
What classifies a residence. Residential buildings are grouped by how plots and units are shared — how many families share the land, walls and access. The type decides the plan form, the bye-laws that apply and the drawings needed.

Detached house / bungalow. One dwelling standing free on its own plot with open margins on all sides. Full privacy, light and air from all four sides; highest land cost per family. The standard subject of submission and working drawings.

Semi-detached house. Two dwellings sharing one common wall, each on its own plot, open on three sides. A compromise: cheaper land than detached, still largely private.

Row houses / tenements. A row of dwellings sharing both side walls, open only at front and back (with a rear margin/court). Typical of housing colonies and industrial townships; planning discipline: every room must still borrow light/air from front, rear or an internal courtyard.

Apartment / flat (block of flats). Many dwellings stacked in storeys around common stairs/lifts on one plot — G+1 in this subject, high-rise in cities. Land cost shared by many families; common areas, parking, fire and services rules enter the bye-laws.

Duplex and twin/group housing. Duplex: one family's rooms spread over two interconnected floors with an internal stair. Group housing: an organised colony of the above types with common open spaces, internal roads and services planned together — the layout plan becomes an extra drawing.

Classification companions. By construction: load-bearing (walls carry loads — low rise) and framed (RCC columns/beams carry loads — any height), detailed in Unit 3. By occupancy, NBC classifies all buildings (residential = Group A) — the occupancy group controls fire, exit and sanitation bye-laws.

Drawing consequence. Type first, plan second: a detached bungalow plan can open windows everywhere; a row-house plan must plan courtyards; an apartment plan must first fix the common staircase and corridor, then arrange flats around it.

h.en: 2.2 Site selection for a residential building
h.gu: 2.2 Site selection for a residential building

body.en:
Why the site is a planning decision. A beautiful plan on a wrong plot fails daily for fifty years. Site selection compares plots on health, access, services, ground and law — before a single room is drawn.

1) Location and surroundings. Quiet, clean, non-industrial neighbourhood; away from marshes, dumping grounds, heavy traffic fumes and flood-prone low land; reasonably near school, market, hospital, workplace and public transport.

2) Soil and ground. Firm, well-drained sub-soil (avoid made-up/filled ground and black cotton stretches where possible) keeps foundations shallow and cheap; high ground table area avoids water-logging; gentle slope drains rain away from the plinth. A site needing deep foundations can cost more than a costlier plot.

3) Access and shape. Direct approach from a public road of adequate width (bye-laws link permissible height to road width); regular, preferably rectangular plot — odd triangles waste area in unusable corners; adequate frontage for entrance, parking and future widening.

4) Services available. Municipal water supply, drainage/sewer line, electricity and storm-water drain at or near the plot; in their absence, budget for a borewell, septic tank/soak pit and longer service connections — all of which also need space on the plot.

5) Legal and bye-law status. Clear title, NA (non-agricultural) permission for construction, zoning (residential zone), permissible FSI and margins of that zone, no road-widening or reservation line cutting the plot, no high-tension line or nala passing through. Verify the plot in the authority's development plan before purchase.

6) Orientation potential and future. Plot long-side facing favourable directions (Unit 2.3 aspect/orientation) so rooms can get morning sun and breeze; scope for future extension vertically (foundation/permission) or horizontally (margin kept free).

The site visit habit. Visit at different times: morning (sun), evening (traffic/noise), and in rain if possible (drainage truth). Photograph levels, neighbouring buildings (they block light/air and show the local water table in their plinths), and existing trees/services to be reused.

h.en: 2.3 Principles of planning — residential and public buildings
h.gu: 2.3 Principles of planning — residential and public buildings

items.syllabus_item: 2.3 Principles of planning for Residential and Public building: Aspect, Prospect, Orientation, Grouping, Privacy, Elegance, Flexibility, Circulation, Furniture requirements, Sanitation, Economy

body.en:
What 'planning' means. Planning arranges rooms (sizes, positions, connections) inside a given plot and budget so the building works — sun, air, movement, privacy and cost simultaneously. The syllabus lists eleven principles; examiners ask them one by one and in application to a line plan.

1) Aspect. The direction a room faces — decided by which walls carry its windows. Kitchen: east (morning sun sterilises, day heat gone by cooking time); bedrooms: south-west/west breeze with sun control; living room: south or south-east pleasant light; study/north light: steady, glare-free (northern sky light). A room's aspect is fixed by the plan forever — its most permanent decision.

2) Prospect. The view from the windows — and how the house presents itself to view. Plan windows towards garden/road/green, away from neighbouring toilets or blank walls; the elevation's pleasant face (Card 2.3's house front) is prospect designed from outside-in.

3) Orientation. Placing the whole building with respect to sun path and prevailing wind (in most of India: breeze from south-west). Long axis preferably east–west so long walls face north–south (less direct sun on large walls), openings catch the breeze, and chajjas/verandahs shade the hot west. Orientation is aspect applied to the whole plot.

4) Grouping. Related rooms together, unrelated separated: kitchen near dining/living but kitchen's store attached; bedrooms clustered in the quiet zone; bath-WC between bedrooms for shared access; drawing room near entrance so guests never cross private rooms. In public buildings: offices near entrance, record/store behind, toilets grouped on one plumbing wall (cheaper and leak-safe).

5) Privacy. Two kinds: privacy of the whole house from the street (entrance lobby, verandah screen, compound wall, window positions not facing the road at eye level) and privacy between rooms (no bedroom opened directly off the living room without a lobby; bathroom doors never face dining/living directly — a short passage breaks the sight line).

6) Elegance. The pleasing overall effect — proportions of elevation, position of openings, roof line, materials and colour. Elegance is planned, not decorated afterwards: symmetric or balanced fenestration and a composed elevation read as one design.

7) Flexibility. Rooms planned to serve changed uses over the building's life: a study that becomes a bedroom, a living room extendable into a verandah, partition (non-load-bearing) walls where future change is likely; in framed structures the column grid itself gives flexibility. Families change faster than buildings.

8) Circulation. The path of movement — horizontal (passages, lobby, verandah) and vertical (staircase, Unit 3). Rules: short, direct, well-lit and ventilated; independent access to every room (never through another room); passage area is necessary waste — roughly 10–15% of floor area is healthy, zero and 30% are both failures (privacy dies at zero, economy at 30).

9) Furniture requirements. Rooms sized and doors/windows placed for the furniture they must hold: bed + wardrobe + passage in bedrooms, dining table circulation, kitchen platform sequence (store–wash–cook–serve). Draw furniture in the line plan and check: door swings clear of beds, window positions free of wardrobe backs, 750–900 mm clear movement lanes.

10) Sanitation. Light, ventilation and cleanliness services planned in: every habitable room windowed (openable area a set fraction of floor area — bye-law, Card 2.4); bath-WC ventilated to outside air (shaft where unavoidable); kitchen smoke/steam escape; plumbing concentrated (grouping) with falls to the drain; damp-proofing, floor slopes to nahani traps, and refuse disposal space. A dark, unventilated room cannot be repaired by paint.

11) Economy. The plan itself is the biggest cost decision: compact (near-square) plans have the least wall length per floor area (walls = money); standard sizes reuse formwork/material sizes; avoid odd shapes, unnecessary passages and oversized rooms; economy never by cutting sanction, ventilation or structure. Economy balances all ten principles above — that is why it is listed last.

For public buildings the same eleven apply with changed weights: grouping by public/semi-public/private zones, circulation wide and fire-safe with clear exits, sanitation in banks of toilets on plumbing walls, flexibility for office re-partitioning, elegance as institutional dignity.

h.en: 2.4 Building bye-laws of the sanctioning authority
h.gu: 2.4 Building bye-laws of the sanctioning authority

items.syllabus_item: 2.4 Building bye-law: 2.4.1 Importance, 2.4.2 Minimum dimensions (plot, built-up, super built-up, plinth, carpet, floor area, FSI/FAR, room sizes, margins, height, passages, ventilation, circulation), 2.4.3 Colour code, 2.4.4 Approval procedure

body.en:
What bye-laws are (2.4.1). Building bye-laws (Development Control Regulations) are the legal rules of the local sanctioning authority — municipal corporation, municipality or urban development authority (in Gujarat, the local body's GDCR under the state town-planning framework, resting on NBC) — controlling what may be built where: land use, coverage, height, margins, light and ventilation. Importance: they protect (i) health — light, air, sanitation minimums; (ii) safety — fire gaps, structural and exit norms; (iii) neighbours — your building may not steal another's light or overload the street's services; (iv) the city plan — roads, reservations, density (FSI). Building without sanction is illegal, uninsurable and demolish-able; a diploma engineer who plans within bye-laws is doing professional work.

The area words (2.4.2) — learn them as measurements. Plot area: area of the land parcel. Built-up area: total covered area of all floors (incl. walls). Plinth area: built-up area of the ground floor measured at plinth level (the plinth-area rate basis of estimates). Floor area: built-up area minus area occupied by walls — usable area of a floor. Carpet area: floor area where a carpet can be laid — excludes walls, bath-WC, passages, verandah: the family's living measure. Super built-up area: carpet area plus proportionate share of common areas (stairs, lift, lobby, terrace shares in apartments) — a sale term, always larger than carpet; honest comparison between flats is by carpet area. FSI (Floor Space Index) / FAR (Floor Area Ratio) — the same ratio:

FSI = (total built-up area of all floors) / (plot area)

FSI 1.0 on a 200 m² plot permits 200 m² total built-up (all floors together). Ground coverage (built-up/plinth footprint ÷ plot area, as %) is controlled separately — FSI can be consumed in fewer taller floors or more low floors within height and margin rules.

Minimum dimensions — the typical control set (learn the pattern; verify your local GDCR numbers). Habitable rooms: floor area ≈ 9.5 m² minimum (one-room units smaller allowed), width ≈ 2.4–3.0 m, height ≈ 2.75–3.0 m clear. Kitchen ≈ 4.5–5.5 m², height ≈ 2.75 m. Bath ≈ 1.8 m² (1.2 × 1.5 m), WC ≈ 1.1 m² (0.9 × 1.2 m), combined bath-WC ≈ 2.8 m²; their height may be ≈ 2.1–2.4 m under a loft/mezzanine practice where allowed. Doors: main ≈ 1.0 × 2.1 m, internal ≈ 0.9 × 2.0 m, bath-WC ≈ 0.75 × 2.0 m (Unit 5 schedule). Windows/ventilation: total openable opening ≈ 1/10 to 1/6 of floor area (local rule), ventilator near ceiling for hot air. Margins (open spaces): front margin by road width (often 3.0–4.5 m), side/rear 1.5–3.0 m scaled with height; passages ≈ 1.0–1.2 m wide minimum; staircase width ≈ 0.9–1.0 m residential, headroom ≥ 2.0–2.1 m; building height linked to road width and margin (taller building = wider road + larger margins = light/air cone protected). Plinth height typically 300–600 mm above ground/road level against rain entry.

Colour code in submission drawings (2.4.3). Authorities prescribe colours so the checking engineer reads the proposal at a glance. The widely used convention: existing work — black/white (or grey); proposed new work — red; work to be demolished — yellow (crossed); drainage/sewer lines — (often) red dotted or as prescribed; water-supply lines — green or blue dotted; plot boundary and margins/setbacks often in distinct heavy colours on the site plan. Exact code varies by authority — the submission set must carry the colour legend used, and the diploma rule is: follow the sanctioning body's current colour schedule, print the legend on the sheet. (Local practice in Gujarat bodies follows this red = proposed convention; always confirm the current GDCR sheet requirements.)

Approval procedure (2.4.4) — the sequence. 1) Engage licensed architect/engineer; prepare submission set (application form, ownership/title documents, plot/NA papers, site plan, plans-elevation-sections, area/FSI statement, structural undertaking as required). 2) Submit online/at the authority with scrutiny fees; the junior engineer scrutinises against zoning, FSI, margins, height, parking and services. 3) Objections/queries are raised in writing → comply and resubmit. 4) Development permission / commencement certificate (rajachitthi) issued with conditions and validity period. 5) Build exactly as sanctioned; intimation of stages/plinth check as prescribed; deviations need revised sanction before execution. 6) On completion: completion report → inspection → Building Use (BU) permission / occupancy certificate; only then lawful occupation, water/sewer connections and sale registration follow smoothly. The working drawings of Unit 3 must match the sanctioned submission set — sanction is a promise the site keeps.

h.en: 2.5 Green building — concept, components and rating
h.gu: 2.5 Green building — concept, components and rating

items.syllabus_item: 2.5 Green Building: 2.5.1 Concept and components, 2.5.2 Evaluation system of various authorities (GRIHA, IGBC)

body.en:
Concept (2.5.1). A green building is designed, built and operated to use less energy, water and materials, generate less waste, and keep occupants healthier over its whole life — site selection to demolition. It is the planning principles of 2.3 with the environment added as a client: orientation and shading cut cooling load; daylight replaces lamps; harvested rain replaces tanker water.

Components — the five working groups. 1) Sustainable site: build on already-developed land, protect trees/topsoil, orient for sun/wind, control dust and erosion during construction, heat-island care (shade/reflective roofs, open-grid paving). 2) Water efficiency: rainwater harvesting (recharge pit/roof storage), low-flow fixtures, dual plumbing/wastewater recycling for flushing and gardening, drought-tolerant landscaping, metering. 3) Energy efficiency: daylighting, natural ventilation, shaded/envelope-insulated walls and roof, solar water heating and rooftop PV, efficient lamps/appliances (star-rated), building form itself first — a well-oriented plan is the cheapest 'green technology'. 4) Materials and resources: local materials (less transport), recycled-content materials (fly-ash bricks/blocks, Unit material link), waste segregation and construction-waste reuse, rapidly renewable materials (bamboo). 5) Indoor environmental quality: fresh-air ventilation, daylight without glare, low-VOC paints/adhesives (VOC = volatile organic compounds that pollute indoor air), thermal and acoustic comfort, views to outside.

Evaluation systems (2.5.2). GRIHA (Green Rating for Integrated Habitat Assessment) — India's national rating by MNRE/TERI: criteria across site, water, energy, materials and indoor quality, scored in points and awarded 1 to 5 stars; mandatory push for government buildings. IGBC (Indian Green Building Council, of CII) — rating families for homes, factories, schools, townships etc., awarding Certified, Silver, Gold, Platinum levels by points in similar credit groups (IGBC Green Homes is the residential one). Both are voluntary market/government-recognised systems — understand them as checklists with points: the design team targets credits (e.g., rainwater harvesting, solar, waste segregation) and documents them for certification after construction.

For the drawing office. Green decisions appear on drawings: orientation and shading devices on the elevation, RWH pit and plumbing separation on the site/services plan, solar panels/heater on the roof plan, material notes in specifications, window sizes serving daylight/ventilation in the schedule. A green claim with no drawing behind it is only a brochure.

h.en: 2.6 Line plan of a single-storey residential building
h.gu: 2.6 Line plan of a single-storey residential building

items.syllabus_item: 2.6 Line plans for Single storey Residential Building as per principles of planning

body.en:
What a line plan is. The first scaled drawing of the idea: walls shown by single (centre) lines (or thin double lines), rooms named with their internal sizes, door positions with swings, window positions, and the overall dimensions — drawn to a convenient scale (1:50 or 1:100) before wall thicknesses and construction detail are added. The detailed/working plan of Unit 3 is a line plan 'grown up': line → wall, name → dimensioned room, swing → scheduled door.

Procedure — plan it in this order. 1) List the client's rooms with bye-law minimum sizes (2.4) plus furniture needs (2.3-9). 2) Group them (2.3-4): public zone (verandah/living) at the entrance, private zone (bedrooms) away, service zone (kitchen/bath-WC) on one plumbing side; fix aspect for each (2.3-1). 3) Set the overall rectangle from plot, margins and FSI (worked in Numerical 2.1). 4) Arrange rooms inside keeping circulation a short central passage/lobby (2.3-8), no room through a room. 5) Place doors (swing clears furniture, privacy sight-lines broken by lobbies), windows (light/ventilation fractions, cross-ventilation: openings on opposite walls), bath-WC ventilators to the rear/duct. 6) Dimension overall and room sizes; check the plan against all eleven principles and bye-laws; only then draw wall thicknesses and develop elevation/section.

Reading the diagram. The line plan in Figure (Card 2.6) shows the method's output: living room at the entrance front (public), kitchen adjacent (grouping, east aspect possible), bedrooms in the quiet rear (privacy), bath-WC sharing one wet corner (sanitation + plumbing economy), door swings arc'd clear of furniture zones, overall dimensions 9000 × 6200 mm outside the plan, north point fixed so aspect decisions can be judged.

Common line-plan faults to hunt in revision. Bedroom through bedroom (circulation); WC door opening straight into dining (privacy/sanitation); kitchen window over no sink position (furniture); dark middle room with no window (bye-law + sanitation); passage eating a quarter of the house (economy); door swing cutting a bed (furniture). One revision pass per principle — eleven quick passes — is the professional habit this unit must create.

title.en: Numerical 2.1 — FSI check: how much can be built on this plot?
title.gu: Numerical 2.1 — FSI check: how much can be built on this plot?

body.en:
Given. Residential plot 12.0 m × 20.0 m (area 240 m²). Permissible FSI = 1.2. Proposed ground floor built-up = 130 m², first floor built-up = 130 m². (Bye-law values assumed for the exercise — verify the current local GDCR.)

Find. (a) Maximum permissible total built-up area. (b) Whether the proposal is within FSI, and how much area remains.

Step 1. Find the permissible total built-up area from FSI.

permissible built-up = FSI × plot area = 1.2 × 240 = 288 m²

Step 2. Add the proposed floors.

proposed total = 130 + 130 = 260 m²

Step 3. Compare and find the balance.

balance = 288 − 260 = 28 m² (proposal is within FSI)

Final answer.

╔ Permissible = 288 m² ; proposed 260 m² is allowed, with 28 m² FSI still unused ╗

Validity check. FSI consumed = 260 / 240 = 1.083 ≤ 1.2 ✓. Also check ground coverage separately: 130 / 240 = 54% — that must satisfy the coverage and margin rules too; FSI alone never sanctions a plan.

title.en: Numerical 2.2 — From built-up area to carpet area, and a ventilation check
title.gu: Numerical 2.2 — From built-up area to carpet area, and a ventilation check

body.en:
Given. A flat has built-up area 78 m². Walls occupy 8% of built-up; bath + WC together 5.6 m²; internal passages 4.2 m²; verandah 3.0 m² (all measured within the built-up). Living room is 4.2 m × 3.6 m with total openable window/door-to-outside area of 1.9 m². (Exercise data.)

Find. (a) Carpet area and carpet efficiency. (b) Whether the living room meets an openable-area rule of 1/10 of floor area.

Step 1. Find the wall area.

walls = 0.08 × 78 = 6.24 m²

Step 2. Subtract walls, bath-WC, passages and verandah from built-up area.

carpet = 78 − 6.24 − 5.6 − 4.2 − 3.0 = 58.96 m² ≈ 59.0 m²

Step 3. Find carpet efficiency.

efficiency = 58.96 / 78 × 100 = 75.6 %

Step 4. Check the living-room openable area.

floor area = 4.2 × 3.6 = 15.12 m² ; required ≥ 15.12 / 10 = 1.51 m² ; provided 1.9 m² ≥ 1.51 m² ✓

Final answer.

╔ Carpet area ≈ 59.0 m² (75.6% of built-up) ; living-room ventilation check passes ╗

Validity check. Carpet efficiency around 70–80% is typical for small flats; below ~65%, walls and passages are eating the home — revisit grouping and circulation (Cards 2.3–2.4).

title.en: Formulae, methods and key data — Unit 2
title.gu: Formulae, methods and key data — Unit 2

body.en:
FSI (= FAR) = total built-up area of all floors / plot areapermissible total built-up = FSI × plot areaground coverage % = plinth (ground built-up) area / plot area × 100floor area = built-up area − wall area ; carpet area = floor area − (bath-WC + passages + verandah)

Order of inclusion. Plot ⊃ built-up/plinth footprint on the ground; per floor: built-up → (minus walls) floor → (minus wet/passage areas) carpet. Super built-up = carpet + share of common areas (sale term). State which area every rate/area statement uses.

q.en: What is the difference between a detached and a semi-detached house?
q.gu: What is the difference between a detached and a semi-detached house?

a.en: Detached: one dwelling free-standing on its plot, open all around. Semi-detached: two dwellings sharing one common wall, each on its own plot.
a.gu: Detached: one dwelling free-standing on its plot, open all around. Semi-detached: two dwellings sharing one common wall, each on its own plot.

q.en: Name any five principles of planning.
q.gu: Name any five principles of planning.

a.en: Aspect, prospect, orientation, grouping, privacy - plus elegance, flexibility, circulation, furniture requirements, sanitation, economy (any five).
a.gu: Aspect, prospect, orientation, grouping, privacy - plus elegance, flexibility, circulation, furniture requirements, sanitation, economy (any five).

q.en: What is aspect? Give the preferred aspect for a kitchen in India.
q.gu: What is aspect? Give the preferred aspect for a kitchen in India.

a.en: The direction a room faces through its openings. Kitchen: east - morning sun, and heat gone before evening cooking (bedrooms favour the breeze side, living room south/south-east).
a.gu: The direction a room faces through its openings. Kitchen: east - morning sun, and heat gone before evening cooking (bedrooms favour the breeze side, living room south/south-east).

q.en: What is FSI? FSI 1.5 is allowed on a 300 m² plot - how much total built-up is permitted?
q.gu: What is FSI? FSI 1.5 is allowed on a 300 m² plot - how much total built-up is permitted?

a.en: FSI = total built-up area of all floors / plot area. Permitted = 1.5 × 300 = 450 m².
a.gu: FSI = total built-up area of all floors / plot area. Permitted = 1.5 × 300 = 450 m².

q.en: Distinguish plinth area, floor area and carpet area.
q.gu: Distinguish plinth area, floor area and carpet area.

a.en: Plinth: ground-floor built-up at plinth level. Floor area: built-up minus walls. Carpet: floor area minus bath-WC, passages and verandah - the usable living area.
a.gu: Plinth: ground-floor built-up at plinth level. Floor area: built-up minus walls. Carpet: floor area minus bath-WC, passages and verandah - the usable living area.

q.en: In a submission drawing, what does red colour usually show?
q.gu: In a submission drawing, what does red colour usually show?

a.en: The proposed new work (existing work black/grey, demolition yellow) - as per the sanctioning authority's colour legend printed on the sheet.
a.gu: The proposed new work (existing work black/grey, demolition yellow) - as per the sanctioning authority's colour legend printed on the sheet.

q.en: What is the last permission before a new building may be occupied?
q.gu: What is the last permission before a new building may be occupied?

a.en: The Building Use (BU) permission / occupancy certificate, issued after completion inspection against the sanctioned drawings.
a.gu: The Building Use (BU) permission / occupancy certificate, issued after completion inspection against the sanctioned drawings.

q.en: Why should bath and WC be grouped on one wall or back-to-back?
q.gu: Why should bath and WC be grouped on one wall or back-to-back?

a.en: Plumbing economy and safety: one soil/water line stack, shorter pipes, fewer leakage points - the sanitation + grouping principles.
a.gu: Plumbing economy and safety: one soil/water line stack, shorter pipes, fewer leakage points - the sanitation + grouping principles.

q.en: What is circulation? What passage share is healthy?
q.gu: What is circulation? What passage share is healthy?

a.en: Movement space (passages, lobby, stairs) connecting rooms so each room is reached independently. Roughly 10-15% of floor area; rooms must never be reached through other rooms.
a.gu: Movement space (passages, lobby, stairs) connecting rooms so each room is reached independently. Roughly 10-15% of floor area; rooms must never be reached through other rooms.

q.en: Name the two Indian green-building rating systems in the syllabus.
q.gu: Name the two Indian green-building rating systems in the syllabus.

a.en: GRIHA (1-5 stars, MNRE/TERI national rating) and IGBC (Certified/Silver/Gold/Platinum levels, CII).
a.gu: GRIHA (1-5 stars, MNRE/TERI national rating) and IGBC (Certified/Silver/Gold/Platinum levels, CII).

q.gu: What is a line plan?

a.en: The first scaled planning drawing: walls as single lines, rooms named with sizes, door swings and windows shown, overall dimensions given - the seed of the working plan.
